title: C++ Basics Quiz
description: 20 questions on data types, loops, time and space complexity, primes and divisors, integer and floating-point division, rounding, and pattern printing.

topics.Data types: char arithmetic, choosing int or long long
topics.Division: int and double division, negatives and %
topics.Rounding: floor, ceil, round, rounding up with ints

questions.e: 'A' is stored as 65, so 'A' + 2 is 67. Storing 67 in a char gives the character 'C', and cout prints a char as a character.

questions.q: You need to store the number 3,000,000,000 (3 billion). Which type is the safe choice?
questions.e: An int usually holds values up to 2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 billion), so 3 billion overflows it. long long goes up to about 9.2 × 10¹⁸.
i takes the values 0, 3, 6 and 9. At 12 the condition i < 10 fails, so the body runs 4 times.
i-- tests the old value, then decreases it. 5 passes and 4 is printed, and so on down to 1, which passes and prints 0. When the old value is 0 the loop stops.
continue skips the rest of the body only when i is 3, so s = 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.e: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, giving n × n steps.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this loop?
questions.c:
for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2)
    cnt++;
questions.e: i doubles every time: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. It passes n after about log₂ n steps.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this loop?
questions.c:
for (int i = 1; i * i <= n; i++)
    cnt++;
questions.e: The loop stops once i is bigger than √n, so it runs about √n times. That is why prime checks and divisor loops use i * i <= n.

questions.q: What does isPrime(1) return, and is that right?
o: true, which is wrong because 1 is not prime
questions.e: For n = 1 the loop never runs (2 * 2 <= 1 is false), so the function returns true. Adding if (n < 2) return false; at the top fixes it.

questions.q: In the Sieve of Eratosthenes, when you reach a prime p, from which number can you start crossing out its multiples?
questions.e: Every smaller multiple k × p (with k < p) has a prime factor smaller than p, so it was already crossed out. The first new one is p × p.
The loop finds the pairs (1, 16), (2, 8) and (4, 4). The pair 4 × 4 is counted once, so the divisors are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16: five of them.
7 / 2 divides two ints, so the decimal part is dropped and you get 3. If either side is a double, as with 2.0, the result is 3.5.
7 / 2 is worked out with ints first (3), and only then stored in d as 3.0. cout prints 3.0 as 3. Write 7.0 / 2 or (double)7 / 2 to get 3.5.
C++ integer division rounds toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3. The remainder takes the sign of the left side: -7 = 2 × (-3) + (-1).
floor always goes down to the next whole number (-3) and ceil always goes up (-2). For negative numbers, down means further from zero.
round moves values that are exactly halfway away from zero: 2.5 becomes 3 and -2.5 becomes -3.

questions.q: a and b are positive ints. Which expression gives a ÷ b rounded up?
questions.e: ceil(a / b) fails because a / b is already cut down to an int before ceil sees it. a / b + 1 is wrong when b divides a exactly. Adding b - 1 first pushes any remainder up to the next whole number.
Row i prints i stars and then a new line: 1, 2 and 3 stars.
The inner loop prints j, which starts again from 1 on every row. Printing i instead would give 1, 22, 333.

questions.q: To print this right-aligned triangle for n = 4, how many spaces come before the stars on row i (rows numbered 1 to n)?
questions.e: Every row is n characters wide. Row i has i stars, so it needs n - i spaces first: 3, 2, 1, 0.
